extracted.intended_audience: folklorists, humor scholars, cultural analysts, and students studying ethnic/genre humor
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Oring's appropriate-incongruity framework to diagnose and interpret specific humor instances (ethnic jokes, cartoons, memes, genre jokes) by identifying incongruous categories, the dimension of their perceived appropriateness, and the cultural beliefs expressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic principle (three-step)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any specific humor instance, identify: (1) the categories that are incongruous in the joke; (2) the dimension along which they are nevertheless appropriate; (3) what social/cultural anxieties or commentaries the appropriate-incongruity expresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these three steps as a basic analytic diagnostic: start by cataloguing the paired categories the joke juxtaposes, determine why the audience might perceive them as 'fitting' despite incongruity, and then connect that perceived fit to broader cultural anxieties or commentaries. Use concrete examples to ground each step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jewish humor: incongruity / appropriate fit / cultural function
rubrics_metrics.description: Incongruous categories: sacred / profane, learned / impractical, suffering / cleverness, victim / survivor. Appropriate fit: Jewish wit is precisely the joining of these — the Talmudic thinker who cannot navigate everyday life, the survivor whose response to disaster is irony. Cultural function: affirms the humor as a coping mode shaped by historical conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing Jewish jokes, show how the joke's incongruous categories are recast as an 'appropriate' fit given historical experience; emphasize examples (Talmudic scholar vs. everyday incompetence, survivor irony) and interpret the coping/affirmation function rather than treating jokes as mere cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frontier humor (Mark Twain, tall tales): incongruity / fit / function
rubrics_metrics.description: Incongruous categories: elevated literary register / crude reality, civilization / wilderness, pretense / actuality. Appropriate fit: frontier life routinely produces such collisions; the humor records the texture of that life. Cultural function: democratic deflation — the frontier laughs at refinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read frontier jokes as indexing lived contradictions between refinement and rough reality; show how the humor's 'appropriate fit' documents and deflates pretension. Use tall-tale exaggeration and Twain examples to demonstrate how incongruity is rooted in social context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Racist cartoons: stereotype vs individual; appropriateness diagnostic
rubrics_metrics.description: Incongruous categories: stereotype / individual, perceived 'essence' / evidence to the contrary. Appropriate fit: the cartoon claims that the stereotype 'fits' some real feature. Critical question: Is the appropriateness real, or is the joke fabricating it? Oring argues that to laugh requires perceiving appropriateness; if the audience rejects the supposed fit, the cartoon fails. Cultural function: much racist humor enforces or affirms stereotype. Some, however, mocks the stereotype itself — depending on framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat racist cartoons as diagnostic: determine whether the audience reads the cartoon as asserting a real fit (thus revealing belief in the stereotype) or as ironic/critical. Note that if the audience does not perceive the fit, the joke will fail or be recoded as critique. Use framing and audience orientation to distinguish enforcement from mockery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blonde jokes: beauty/intellect incongruity and cultural reinforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Incongruous categories: beautiful/desirable woman / stupid/incapable. Appropriate fit: culturally encoded suspicion that beauty/sexuality and intellect are inversely related; laughter affirms a misogynist stereotype. Cultural function: restoration of (false) hierarchy in which conventionally attractive women are demoted on intellectual grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse blonde jokes by showing how the perceived 'fit' between beauty and lack of intellect depends on cultural assumptions; highlight the joke's role in reinforcing gendered hierarchies rather than as benign silliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet / meme humor: format-enabled appropriate-incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: Incongruous categories: any cultural elements pulled from disparate domains. Appropriate fit: the meme format itself enables fast appropriate-incongruity production — any image can be paired with any caption to reveal unexpected fits. Cultural function: rapid testing of cultural fits across communities; memes that 'stick' have particularly strong appropriate-incongruity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing memes, focus on how the medium's affordances (recombinability, speed) create and test perceived fits; examine which communities find the fit compelling and why. Consider virality as a marker of particularly salient appropriate-incongruity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oring's diagnostic principle for ethnic humor (four assessment steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: To assess an ethnic joke: (1) What is the supposed appropriateness? (E.g., 'the stereotype really fits this group.'); (2) Does the audience actually perceive that appropriateness, or are they laughing for other reasons (in-group bonding, transgression-thrill, simple absurdity)?; (3) If the audience perceives the appropriateness, what does that say about their beliefs?; (4) If the audience doesn't perceive the appropriateness, the joke either fails (no fit perceived) or is being read as commentary on the stereotype rather than affirmation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these four steps sequentially to decide whether an ethnic joke functions to assert a stereotype, to critique it, or to serve other social functions. Pay special attention to audience composition (in-group vs out-group) and alternative laughter motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive problem of racist humor: laughter as belief-diagnostic
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughing at a racist joke requires perceiving the stereotype as appropriate to the target. This perception is itself a substantive belief. Therefore, 'I laughed but I don't believe the stereotype' is incoherent unless one is laughing at something else (the joke's structure, the absurdity, in-group transgression). This makes laughter ethically diagnostic, not innocent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating racist humor, treat audience laughter as evidence to be interrogated: is it indicating belief, complicity, or a different laughter motive? Beware of claims of harmless laughter without examining what exactly the audience registered as 'appropriate.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic demands of the appropriate-incongruity approach
rubrics_metrics.description: For any specific humor instance: don't just identify the joke's structure; identify what categories are incongruous; identify what makes them appropriate to the audience; identify what cultural beliefs or anxieties the appropriateness depends on; read the joke as testimony about the audience's worldview, not just as standalone art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow this checklist during analysis. Avoid treating jokes as purely formal objects; always link structure to social context and audience perception. Use ethnographic or contextual evidence where possible to support claims about audience belief or anxiety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic questions (practical checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: What categories does the joke present as appropriately incongruous?; What background belief or cultural anxiety must the audience hold for the appropriateness to register?; Does the audience perceive the appropriateness, or are they laughing for different reasons?; What does laughter (or its absence) reveal about audience worldview?; Is the humor reinforcing the connection or critically exhibiting it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these explicit questions as a practical rubric when evaluating individual jokes or humorous artifacts. Answer each question with evidence (textual, performative, audience reaction) and note alternative readings where applicable.
